---
title: Buoyancy flow (2D)
---

Two unequal warm plumes rise and interact in a closed square. Their scalar
field creates upward buoyancy, and the resulting incompressible flow transports
that scalar.
All backends use no-slip velocity walls and zero normal scalar derivative.

| Backend | Coupled flow implementation | Differentiable inputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PhiFlow | Semi-Lagrangian transport, explicit diffusion, and pressure projection. | State and physics parameters |
| JAX-CFD | Native Van Leer momentum and scalar transport, explicit diffusion, and closed-wall pressure projection. | State and physics parameters |
| INS.jl | Native Boussinesq model, centered transport, RK4, and closed-wall transform pressure projection. | State |
| WaterLily | Native momentum and pressure routines, with conservative upwind scalar transport and two-stage coupling added by the adapter. | State and physics parameters |
| Oceananigans | Native nonhydrostatic buoyancy model, third-order upwind advection, RK3, and spectral pressure projection. | State |

The Julia backends initially run on CPU. Each backend generates its own
fine-resolution reference; the physical problem and training recipe are shared,
but the numerical discretizations differ.

JAX-CFD uses Float64 internally to avoid reverse-mode underflow in the native
Van Leer limiter at the plume's small tails; its public state remains Float32.

WaterLily and Oceananigans use Enzyme reverse-mode differentiation; INS.jl uses
Zygote with the library's native operator adjoints. Oceananigans uses
an equivalent separable Neumann pressure inverse because its native FFTW path
lacks Enzyme support. Forward simulation and derivatives use the same pressure
implementation. Its adapter pins Julia 1.12.6 to avoid the reverse-mode
compilation crash observed with Julia 1.11.7 in the Python–Julia runtime.

The benchmark trains a small convolutional neural network to correct velocity
after each solver interval. A streamfunction makes these corrections
divergence-free with zero normal wall velocity. The scalar remains solver-driven.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    S[Velocity and scalar] --> P[Coupled solver step]
    P --> N[Neural velocity correction]
    N --> S
    N --> L[Compare with restricted fine reference]
    L -. Training gradient through the rollout .-> N
```

The default uses a 64² coarse grid and a 128² reference grid, with viscosity
and scalar diffusivity both 0.0005. Each correction interval contains eight
solver steps of 0.005; 100 intervals evolve the flow to time 4. Training uses
256 optimizer updates across four training trajectories. Seed 0 retains the
original two-plume initial condition; seeds 2, 3, and 4 add broader position
variation (±0.04 domain units), width variation (±15%), and amplitude variation
(±15%). Each group of four updates visits every trajectory once in shuffled
order, using independently shuffled eight-interval windows within each trajectory.
Normalization remains fixed from training case 0 to isolate the effect of added
data. Validation seed 1 and held-out test seed 100 retain their original initial
conditions. Every training reference is checked independently for time refinement.

The full validation rollout selects among checkpoints at updates 0, 64, 128,
192, and 256; update 0 is the initial zero-correction model. Every run completes
all 256 updates, even when validation selects an earlier checkpoint. Only the
selected model is evaluated on the test trajectory.

Solver-in-the-loop training minimizes a recurrent trajectory loss, with gradients
through the solver. Held-out rollouts compare the trained corrector against the
uncorrected coarse solver and report velocity and scalar errors separately.
Only the corrector is trained; the uncorrected baseline and fine reference
require forward simulation only.

References come from the same solver at finer spatial and temporal resolution.
The experiment checks reference time refinement, restart equivalence, and
end-to-end finite differences before reporting training results. The benchmark
measures rollout accuracy and training cost within a budget suitable for CI;
these measurements do not require solver-in-the-loop training to win.

This setup is inspired by [Um et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00016).
It is a bounded benchmark, not a reproduction of their full training campaign.
Results and full-field plots appear here when benchmark artifacts are generated.

```bash
mosaic run -p buoyancy-grid --suites forward,gradient,cost,optimization -s phiflow
mosaic run -p buoyancy-grid --suites forward,gradient,cost,optimization -s jax-cfd
mosaic run -p buoyancy-grid --suites forward,gradient,cost,optimization -s ins-jl
mosaic run -p buoyancy-grid --suites forward,gradient,cost,optimization -s waterlily
mosaic run -p buoyancy-grid --suites forward,gradient,cost,optimization -s oceananigans
```
